name: India's Youth: Jobs, Aspirations & Possibilities
description: Join us for a lecture about a number that should be reshaping how we think about India's future:The population of Indian students aged 15 and above doubled in two decades, from 60 million in 2004-05 to 120 million in 2023-24.About the LectureThose numbers above signal a staggering rise in aspiration for upward mobility among young Indians, despite the social disadvantages many of them face. It also means India has the potential to propel itself to the forefront of the knowledge economy — if the quality of education improves at every level.But there's a harder truth underneath the aspiration: research shows slow growth of regular, decent jobs in India, especially in manufacturing and high-value services. Not only are the country's long-term growth prospects at risk, but historically entrenched inequalities could get reinforced in the labour market rather than dissolved by it.This lecture makes the case that India's future growth will have to be built much more on incomes generated within the country than on export demand from abroad, a virtuous cycle of more jobs, higher incomes, and greater domestic demand.The session explores:Why the doubling of India's student population is both an opportunity and a warning signWhat the data shows about the slow growth of decent jobs in manufacturing and high-value servicesHow historically determined inequalities risk being reinforced, rather than resolved, in the labour marketWhy domestic demand, not exports may be the key to India's next phase of growthAbout the SpeakerJayan Jose Thomas is a Professor of Economics at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi, where he has taught since July 2010. He has also served as a Member of the State Planning Board, Government of Kerala. His research addresses development problems related to labour and industrialisation from a macroeconomic perspective, spanning the Indian economy, international development and macroeconomic theory. He previously held a four-year academic position at the National University of Singapore. His research has appeared in journals including World Development, Development and Change, and Economic and Political Weekly, and he contributes regularly to The Hindu.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Inside The Minds of Child Serial Offenders
description: Join us for a lecture that challenges one of our most protected assumptions: Are children always innocent? Or can a young mind knowingly choose violence, deception and repeated criminal behaviour?About the LectureThis unLecture ventures into the unsettling world of children who became serial offenders, pushing past conventional ideas about childhood, innocence and responsibility. Beginning with the fundamentals of child psychology and Kohlberg's theory of moral development, the session examines how children understand right and wrong, when behaviour is merely impulsive, and when it may cross into malicious intent and criminal culpability.Through four to five compelling case studies of child serial killers and repeat offenders from diverse social and economic backgrounds, we'll reconstruct their offences, trace how they were eventually apprehended, and identify the psychological and situational factors that may have shaped their conduct — without reducing violent behaviour to any single cause.The session explores:How Kohlberg's theory of moral development helps explain a child's understanding of right and wrongReal case studies of child serial offenders and how investigators pieced together their patternsThe neuropsychological, behavioural and environmental factors that shape early violent behaviourHow families, schools and institutions can recognise warning signs before childhood deviance escalates into persistent violenceAbout the SpeakerVidushi Jain is a UGC-NET-qualified criminologist, researcher and child-safety advocate. She currently works as a Research Assistant in Criminology, Law and Forensics at the National Forensic Sciences University, Delhi Campus, where she is also pursuing her PhD in Criminology, researching adolescent relationships under the POCSO Act and the complexities of strengthening child-protection mechanisms. A Gold Medallist in Criminology with a specialisation in Human Rights, she brings a background in Media and Communication to her research. She has worked with a Child Rights NGO (Project CACA, Delhi) and UNICEF on child education projects, contributed to the NCPCR's POCSO Department, and trained over 12,000 teachers, 3,000 parents and support staff across 200+ schools pan-India. She has also worked on a national-level research project with over 300 police officers on cybercrime investigations, and with acid-attack survivors on their rehabilitation.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. description: Join us for a lecture that will (most likely) change how you hear every song you already know. About the LectureMost of us think of a track as one thing, a song, a feeling, a mood. description: Grounds for Thought: August 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesFour Thursday evenings. Four very different conversations. Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shops. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does.6th August: Shambhavi TiwariPossessed: The Ghost, The Asylum, The Priest, and the PeopleWhen someone in rural India is "possessed by a ghost," they encounter not just their family and their priest, but eventually — often — a psychiatrist. Two completely different frameworks for what has gone wrong, and what healing looks like. This session uses spirit possession across Indian cultural contexts to examine what happens when indigenous knowledge systems and clinical medicine cross paths. PhD researcher Shambhavi Tiwari, who has spent years in this space, asks: superstition, myth, knowledge system, or something else entirely?13th August: Dr. Vishwas ChitaleZoom In, Zoom Out: What India's Climate Risk Looks Like at Ground LevelEveryone has heard the national climate numbers. But zoom into a district, and the picture changes entirely — neighbouring areas with opposite risk profiles, and disaster plans built on averages too coarse to catch where the real danger sits. Dr. Vishwas Chitale, Fellow at CEEW, will walk us through India's climate risk from the national level down to your own neighbourhood — and then hand the tool to the room. Participants will pull up their own hometown's actual climate risk profile live, using CRAVIS, CEEW's climate intelligence platform. You'll leave having done a small piece of the research yourself.20th August: Antara ChakrabartyFrom Village to Viral: How Folk Music Got a Second LifeA seventeenth-century Sufi verse now has a hundred million YouTube views. The songs of Lalon Fakir, Bengal's wandering poet-saint, are uniting two Bengals and two centuries through a single melody. This session traces folk music's remarkable journey — from Punjab's Sufi shrines and Bengal's riverside Baul gatherings to studio stages and streaming platforms — and asks the questions nobody quite wants to answer. Who owns a folk song? What happens when heritage becomes entertainment? Does something get lost in translation, or does it simply learn a new way to survive? Expect live music, a few surprises, and a fresh way of listening to songs you may already love.27th August: Sunaina SaxenaWhat is a Clean Street Worth?Why are two seemingly identical houses priced so differently? This session explores one of environmental economics' most elegant tools, hedonic pricing, to answer a question most of us have never thought to ask: does the cleanliness of a neighbourhood have a measurable economic value? Through stories, discussion, and simple examples, researcher Sunaina Saxena explores how clean streets, reliable waste collection, and a healthy living environment become embedded in housing prices — and what that reveals about our cities and the choices we make about where we live.

name: Forwarded as Received: Misinformation 101
description: Join us for a lecture that asks a question with no comfortable answer:If the people deciding what counts as true are working from the same broken information as everyone else, who do we trust to hold the line?About The Lecture"Fake news" was always too small a phrase. It suggested a fabricated story, a fact-check, a correction — a problem that could, in theory, be solved. What we're actually living through is something else: real photographs stripped of context, selective truths, political insinuation, and claims repeated in enough WhatsApp groups until they stop needing to be true at all.Drawing on her book "Forwarded as Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True," this lecture looks past the individual act of falling for a hoax and toward the larger machinery — how misinformation and malinformation move through digital platforms, political campaigns, and even bureaucratic institutions, shaping not just what people believe, but who gets counted, trusted, or excluded.This isn't a lecture about how other people get fooled. It's about how the very systems built to establish "the facts" — platforms, institutions, public systems — can become vulnerable to the same distortions they claim to correct.About the SpeakerSaadia Azim is the author of "Forwarded as Received: How Misinformation Turns Viral, Violent and True" (Simon & Schuster India), which examines how misinformation moves through everyday social behaviour, politics, media and technology to acquire the force of public truth. She is Chief Operating Officer of the Government of West Bengal's Digital Public Service Delivery Programme, a former journalist, and an Internet Society Mid-Career Fellow. Her work focuses on misinformation, digital governance, algorithmic power, public trust and democratic behaviour in India and the Global South.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi.
